newsitem.title: USA: New safety rules unveiled for Alaska oil tankers.
newsitem.headline: New safety rules unveiled for Alaska oil tankers.

text.p: Starting next year, better escort tugs will be stationed in Prince William Sound to improve the safety of oil tankers traveling in Alaskan waters that were fouled by the 1989 Exxon Valdez spill, state and industry officials said on Monday.

The plan, unveiled at the conclusion of an 18-month tanker traffic safety study, will include a new, high-powered tug stationed at the entrance of the sound and experiments with sophisticated new tractor tugs designed for better maneuverability than standard tugs.

The study was conducted for the U.S. Coast Guard, Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation, the oil and shipping companies and for the Prince William Sound Regional Citizens Advisory Council, an oversight panel established by Congress after the Exxon Valdez spill.

Current safety rules -- including escort requirements, tanker speed limits and other measures imposed after the Exxon Valdez disaster -- have cut collision and grounding risks by three-quarters, the tanker-safety study said.
The most effective safety measure in Prince William Sound has been the use of escort tugs, which are equipped to rescue troubled tankers and respond to spills, the study said.

Major risks that remain, according to the study, include human error among those piloting the tankers and escort vessels, power losses in tankers that are too big to be rescued by tugs in bad weather and possible collisions between oil vessels and fishing boats.
Risks in Prince William Sound are compounded when there is ice in the tanker lanes, the study said.

Just before the Exxon Valdez tanker struck a reef and spilled 11 million gallons of its cargo, ship captain Joseph Hazelwood had ordered the vessel to exit normal transit lanes to avoid floating ice from a nearby glacier.
The oil industry plans several upgrades to the escort system and will announce its investment programs in early 1997, said Roger Gale, president of BP Shipping Co. USA.

Those plans include the more sophisicated escort tugs, long advocated by environmentalists. "There is a place for tractor tugs. I won't say that every tug we have will be a tractor tugs. But there will be tractor tugs, eventually," Gale said.
BP produces about half of the 1.4 million to 1.5 million gallons of crude oil that flows through the trans-Alaska pipeline each day and is unloaded at the Prince William Sound port of Valdez.
Meanwhile, the state, Coast Guard and oil industry have already started a safety program to keep oil tankers and fishing vessels apart, said Tex Edwards, president of the citizens advisory council.
